The paper considers the problem of electromagnetic radiation and scattering from perfectly conducting bodies of revolution of arbitrary shape.
The mathematical formulation is an integro-differential equation, obtained from the potential integrals plus boundary conditions at the body.
The solution is effected by the method of moments, and the results are expressed in terms of generalized network parameters.
A computer program for computing the generalized impedance matrix of an arbitrary body of revolution is included.
The expansion functions chosen for the moment solutions are harmonic in the azimuthal angle and subsectional in the contour length variable.
Due to rotational symmetry, the solution becomes a Fourier series in the azimuthal angle, with each term uncoupled to every other term.
The paper presents computations for radiation from apertures and plane-wave scattering from a conducting sphere and a cone-sphere.

The impedance elements, currents, radiation patterns, and scattering patterns for the conducting sphere are computed both from the general program and the classical eigenfunction solution, showing good agreement.
The cone-sphere example illustrates the application of the general program to problems not solvable by classical methods.
The matrix method allows for efficient computation of the behavior of a conducting body for arbitrary excitation, by inverting the generalized impedance matrix.
The paper uses numerical integration techniques, approximating the triangle functions by piecewise constant and linear functions, to evaluate the impedance matrix elements.
The radiation field is computed using a linear functional of the current, with the measurement matrix derived from the excitation matrix using reciprocity.
The Fourier series expansion in the azimuthal angle decouples the problem into a set of independent modes, which can be solved separately.
The subsectional triangle functions used for the current expansion provide a piecewise-linear approximation that converges about twice as fast as a step approximation.
The paper demonstrates the advantages of the matrix method in terms of computational efficiency and the ability to handle arbitrary body shapes.
